title: Why Apple's Stock Slide Could Continue - Barron's

https://www.barrons.com/articles/why-apples-stock-slide-could-continue-1542454201 Why Apple’s Stock Slide Could Continue By Nov. 17, 2018 6:30 a.m. ET Order Reprints Text size
What a rotten few weeks for Apple investors.
Not long ago, the iPhone maker was the toast of the market as the first U.S. company worth more than $1 trillion. Through early October, shares were up nearly 40% on the year.
Then it all fell apart. Apple’s stock plunged 17%, wiping out nearly $190 billion in shareholder value.
It wasn’t supposed to be this way. In September, Apple (ticker: AAPL) released the $999 iPhone XS and the $1,099 iPhone XS Max, followed by the midrange $749 iPhone XR in October. The pundits predicted blockbuster success for the new devices, with the XR singled out as the best value iPhone ever.
But cracks in the narrative began to form with Apple’s earnings report earlier this month. The company gave disappointing sales guidance for the critical holiday quarter and, in a surprising move, said it would no longer offer unit sales data for its products. Several analysts speculated that the reduction in transparency could be a signal that iPhone sales have peaked.
For investors willing to connect the dots, the big clues came this week when two key suppliers essentially singled out Apple for a sudden shortfall in component orders.
On Monday, Lumentum Holdings (LITE) reduced its quarterly sales forecast by 17%, saying a large customer cut orders for its 3-D sensing laser diode products, a key component for Apple’s FaceID sensor. At an investor conference later that day, Lumentum CEO Alan Lowe said the “lead customer” was asking for expedited shipments at the beginning of the month, before cutting its orders about a week later. Lumentum’s chief financial officer later referred to the same customer as its largest customer, which can only be interpreted in one way: Apple. In Lumentum’s annual report, filed in August, the company lists Apple as its top customer, accounting for 30% of total sales.
A Lumentum spokesperson declined to comment on whether Apple was the customer in question.
On Tuesday, wireless chip maker Qorvo (QRVO) also lowered its financial guidance for its current quarter, citing weaker demand for “flagship smartphones.” Qorvo went out of its way to tell investors two other portions of its business—China-based phone makers and infrastructure defense products—were on track with prior expectations. That left Apple as the obvious culprit. The iPhone maker made up 36% of Qorvo sales per its annual report.
Qorvo did not respond to a request for comment, and Apple declined to comment on the Qorvo and Lumentum guidance cuts.
New Street Research analyst Pierre Ferragu, who downgraded Apple to Sell in August, says he now has more conviction on his call. “The news flow of recent weeks really supports well our perspective,” Ferragu wrote in an email to Barron’s. “The disappointing performance of the iPhone XR shows….High-end buyers are happy to spend more for a fancier phones. It is much less true for budget buyers.” Newsletter Sign-up
Ferragu has a price target of $165 on Apple stock, the lowest on Wall Street. He says Apple’s current cycle is similar to what happened with the iPhone 6S and 6S Plus in 2015 to 2016, when the popularity of prior models had pulled demand forward. Weak demand for the 6S model year sparked a painful selloff in Apple shares. The stock fell 32% from peak to trough before beginning the recovery that culminated in the trillion-dollar market value this summer.
That selloff is a good way to think about Apple’s downside in the months ahead, though there are key differences this time around. Notably, Apple finally seems focused on services like iCloud and music streaming, and revenues are accelerating there. Despite the selloff, no one has suggested that customers are any less pleased with their Apple phones. In fact, the problem may be the phones are so good that fewer folks feel compelled to upgrade.
Apple executives often cite how iPhones have an industry-leading 98% customer satisfaction rate.
Marcelo Lima, a hedge fund manager at Heller House, sees a big opportunity for Apple to increasingly monetize its existing install base of over a billion active devices.
“Apple obviously has growth challenges because the iPhone is quite saturated, and there’s only so much they can keep pushing pricing,” Lima wrote in an email. “I subscribe to my iPhone; I pay [about] $60 a month and can get a new iPhone every year. What if Apple increased that and bundled original video content, music, and other services? I bet a lot of people would subscribe to that.”
Another key difference from prior down cycles is that Apple is more committed to buybacks and dividends that could set a floor in the stock price. The company has $123 billion in net cash (cash minus debt), which executives have vowed to get down to near zero by increasing capital returns to shareholders.
So is Apple, down 17% from its high, now a buy? Maybe not yet.
In the early 1990s, Goldman Sachs analyst Dan Benton, who later ran a large hedge fund, wrote a memo outlining his rules for successful technology investing that was avidly passed around Wall Street. The list downplayed valuations, for two key factors: 1) “sell technology stocks when estimates are being reduced,” and 2) “buy technology stocks only for positive earnings surprises.”
Using those maxims as a guide, investors should probably wait until the rest of Wall Street fully appreciates Apple’s weak product cycle.
Ferragu predicts that iPhone unit shipments will fall 9% in fiscal 2019, which is in the same ballpark as the 8% drop in 2016. For now, Wall Street analysts are expecting only a 2% decline in fiscal-2019 iPhone unit sales. If Ferragu is correct again, then there is a good bit of downside to go. Using the nearly 30% drop from 2015 to 2016, Apple could bottom out in the mid-$160s, down 16% from Friday’s close.
At that point, we would officially call Apple a bargain.
